steps.why: Both are definitions the examiner checks word by word: entropy needs disorder of a system, and heat capacity needs one degree.
common_mistakes: Defining heat capacity per gram — that is specific heat capacity.
Writing that entropy is a form of energy. It is a measure of disorder, with units J K⁻¹.
steps.memory_tip: S for scatter: the more scattered the particles, the higher the entropy. C answers one question: how much heat for one degree?
steps.margin_note: Two short definitions; one or two lines each is enough.

lines.text: Absolute entropy: counted from S = 0 at 0 K; S° quoted at 298 K

steps.why: The third law fixes S = 0 for a pure, perfectly crystalline substance at 0 K, so a real total (absolute) entropy can be counted up from that zero. An absolute entropy exists at every temperature; 298 K is simply the temperature at which standard values are tabulated, not part of what makes the entropy absolute. The tabulated value has its own name, the standard molar entropy S°, so the marked line gives both parts in order: what makes the entropy absolute, then the conditions under which its standard value is quoted. The source book prints the standard state as 273 K; standard thermodynamic data are reported at 298 K, so this card writes 298 K.
common_mistakes: Writing 273 K for the standard-state value — standard molar entropies S° are tabulated at 298 K.
Leaving out per mole — S° is quoted for one mole.
Saying an absolute entropy exists only at 298 K. It exists at every temperature; 298 K is only the temperature at which the standard values are tabulated.
steps.memory_tip: Absolute means counted from a true zero: S = 0 at 0 K for a perfect crystal.
steps.margin_note: Name the third-law zero first, then give S° for one mole at 298 K.
